\subsection{Main comparison}
\resulttable{CIC17_main_b010_paper.tex}{CIC-IDS2017, label budget 10\%, delay 1 window.}{tab:cic17}
\resulttable{IDS18_main_b010_paper.tex}{CSE-CIC-IDS2018, label budget 10\%, delay 1 window.}{tab:ids18}
\resulttable{UNSW_main_b010_paper.tex}{UNSW-NB15 (DoS, Reconnaissance, Shellcode, Worms held out of training), label budget 10\%.}{tab:unsw}

\textbf{CIC-IDS2017} (\cref{tab:cic17}, \cref{fig:time}). \nova{} has the highest OW-F1 (0.768) and AUT
(0.858). The closest baseline is CBRS replay (0.756 and 0.838; paired Wilcoxon $p < 0.001$); every other method is
at least 12 points lower. CBRS detects slightly more attacks (detection F1 0.861 against 0.854, unknown AUROC 0.874
against 0.872), but it does so at a false-positive rate of 4.5\% against 2.8\%: \nova{} sends 38\% fewer benign
flows to the analyst. The static model, which never sees a label, ends at 0.311 because every attack class in the
stream is new to it.

\textbf{CSE-CIC-IDS2018} (\cref{tab:ids18}). \nova{} and CBRS replay tie on OW-F1 (0.722) and AUT (0.869).
\nova{} is better in 51 of the 70 windows ($p = 0.003$), but CBRS is ahead by three points on average over the
last 24 windows, and \nova{} varies more across seeds (0.655 to 0.793). On the other metrics \nova{} is ahead:
detection F1 0.815 against 0.788, false-positive rate 3.1\% against 4.8\%, and maximum forgetting 0.007 against
0.034.

\textbf{UNSW-NB15} (\cref{tab:unsw}, \cref{fig:time-unsw}). Here most adaptive methods end \emph{below} the
static model (0.499): CBRS replay reaches 0.327, continual replay 0.357 and uncertainty sampling 0.243. The
per-flow predictions show why. These methods learn Exploits and Fuzzers, but every flow of these classes is
then rejected as \unk{}, because the open-world thresholds were calibrated on the January reference set and the
February traffic of the same classes lies outside them. Classes that the model has learned are no longer
credited for \unk{}, so the rejections count as errors. \nova{} recalibrates each learned class on recent
labelled flows that it did not train on (the calibration store) and reaches 0.509 OW-F1 and 0.595 AUT, ahead of
the static model ($p = 0.03$) and guarded selective retraining (0.493, $p = 0.007$). We confirmed this
mechanism with one additional run set after the main results, leaving the method unchanged. Without the
calibration store, \nova{} also scores 0 on Exploits and Fuzzers, and it falls to 0.418 OW-F1 and 0.418 AUT
(false-positive rate 9.1\%). This component cost only 1.9 points in the CIC-IDS2017 ablation, where the training
and stream traffic of each learned class are closer. It also has the highest
detection F1 (0.860) and the lowest false-positive rate (6.6\% against 7.6--19.0\%). Every method flags all
UNSW-NB15 attack flows (detection recall 1.0), so on this dataset the methods differ in false positives and in
naming the attack class, not in missed attacks.

\textbf{Self-training.} INSOMNIA, which labels half of each window with its own nearest-centroid estimator, has
the highest false-positive rate on both CIC datasets (12.4\% and 25.7\%) and the largest forgetting on
CSE-CIC-IDS2018 (0.142): pseudo-label errors on unseen classes are fed back into training.

\subsection{Label budget}
\Cref{tab:budget} repeats the comparison with 1\% of each window labelled (40 flows per window). The
configuration is unchanged. The methods that need no labels are omitted, since their results do not depend on
the budget.

On CIC-IDS2017 the lead of \nova{} grows from 1.2 to 9.0 OW-F1 points (0.651 against 0.561 for CBRS replay) and
from 2.0 to 6.5 AUT points (0.820 against 0.755). \nova{} loses 0.117 OW-F1 when the budget shrinks tenfold, CBRS
replay 0.195. Unknown-attack AUROC stays at 0.855 for \nova{} but falls to 0.775 for CBRS replay. On
CSE-CIC-IDS2018, where the two methods tie at 10\%, \nova{} leads at 1\% (0.570 against 0.536, AUT 0.830 against
0.811, $p = 0.002$).

On UNSW-NB15 \nova{} is behind at 1\%: 0.469 against 0.504 for periodic retraining, and 0.48 for continual replay
and guarded selective retraining. The per-class results show that this lead comes from \emph{not} learning.
With 40 labels per window, periodic retraining never collects the five labels per class it needs to learn the
four held-out classes (in all three seeds its last model still leaves out DoS and Reconnaissance as too rare, and
has no Shellcode or Worms labels). It keeps rejecting them as \unk{}, which the metric credits in full (per-class F1 0.99 to
1.00), while it scores 0 on Exploits and Fuzzers, like the static model. \nova{} spends its labels on novel flows,
so it does learn DoS and Reconnaissance. In UNSW-NB15, however, these overlap heavily with Exploits, and in the first
seed 38\% of the DoS flows scored after DoS was learned are labelled Exploits. A class that is learned but confused scores lower than a
class that stays \unk{}. At the same time, \nova{} halves the false-positive rate (9.7\% against 15.7--18.7\%)
and has the highest detection F1 (0.807 against at most 0.721).

\subsection{Ablation}
\resulttable{CIC17_ablation_b010_paper.tex}{Ablation on CIC-IDS2017 (budget 10\%): \nova{} with one component removed.}{tab:ablation}

Removing any one component lowers OW-F1 (\cref{tab:ablation}). The guard matters most: without it OW-F1
drops by 5.6 points to 0.712, although detection F1 (0.873) and unknown AUROC (0.924) rise. Without the hold-out
check, more updates are deployed. They flag more attack flows (detection recall 0.836 against 0.799) but name the
right class less often (open-world attack macro-recall 0.640 against 0.685), and binary detection does not
penalise naming the wrong class. The novelty-weighted query is next (0.726, $-4.2$). It mainly
improves unknown detection (unknown AUROC 0.826 without it). Recency weighting ($-2.3$), the calibration store
($-1.9$; unknown AUROC 0.830) and the class-balanced memory ($-1.9$) follow. Label propagation changes OW-F1 least
($-1.2$) but keeps the false-positive rate down (3.6\% without it, 2.8\% with it).

\subsection{Open-world detector}
Replacing the class-conditional $k$-NN detector by the distance to the nearest class centroid lowers OW-F1 from 0.311 to 0.178 for the static model and from 0.768 to 0.712 for \nova{}. Unknown
AUROC drops from 0.605 to 0.520 and from 0.872 to 0.840. A single centroid cannot follow multi-modal classes:
benign traffic in particular consists of many protocol and application modes. With the centroid detector, the
static model labels almost every attack as benign (detection F1 0.012). The $k$-NN detector is therefore useful
even without adaptation, and every method in \cref{tab:cic17,tab:ids18,tab:unsw} uses it.

\subsection{Neural classifier}
With a two-layer MLP in place of gradient boosting (\cref{tab:mlp}), \nova{} keeps the lowest false-positive rate
(3.3\% against 4.7\% for CBRS replay) and the highest detection F1 (0.865 against 0.824), and both methods have the
same AUT (0.831 against 0.833). \nova{} is better in 49 of 70 windows. Its stream-level OW-F1, however, is clearly
lower (0.622 against 0.711). Per-class F1 shows why: the two methods differ mostly on short-lived web
attacks: XSS (0.09 against 0.68 per-class F1) and Brute Force (0.28 against 0.47) each appear in only a few
windows, so they move the per-window curve little but carry a full class weight in macro-F1. In our
implementation, recency weighting is not applied to the MLP, which takes no sample weights. We therefore do not
claim that \nova{}'s accuracy advantage carries over to neural classifiers; its lower false-positive rate does.

\resulttable{CIC17_model-mlp_b010_paper.tex}{CIC-IDS2017 with an MLP classifier (budget 10\%).}{tab:mlp}
